title: Aileen Wuornos
wiki_lead:
Aileen Carol Wuornos (; née  Pittman; February 29, 1956 – October 9, 2002) was an American serial killer who, while engaging in street prostitution along highways in Florida between 1989 and 1990, robbed and killed seven men who picked her up. She initially testified that the first man she killed, Richard Mallory, had raped her and that the trauma of his assault had influenced her to kill the others. In a 2001 court petition, she instead wrote her motive was robbery in all seven deaths. In a later conversation with documentarian Nick Broomfield that she believed was not being recorded, she said she killed Mallory and "some others" in self-defense, explaining she had lied to hasten her execution and avoid more time on death row. After over ten years on death row, she was executed by lethal injection in 2002.
After her mother abandoned her at age four, Wuornos grew up with her grandparents and was reportedly abused by her grandfather. She became pregnant by 14 and was living on her own by 15, supporting herself through prostitution. A statewide search after the killings ended with her arrest in January 1991. Her girlfriend since 1986, Tyria Moore, assisted investigators in securing a confession to gain immunity. A jury convicted Wuornos of Mallory's murder in 1992; she entered guilty or no contest pleas in five other cases. In 1992, evidence emerged post-trial that Mallory spent ten years in a prison mental institution after a 1957 attempted-rape conviction.
Wuornos ending her appeals prevented the Florida Supreme Court from ruling on Mallory's criminal history. Despite objections that she was mentally ill, her execution proceeded after psychiatrists selected by Governor Jeb Bush concluded that she was competent. Portrayals of her life include an opera, two Broomfield documentaries, and Monster (2003).

Early life
Born Aileen Carol Pittman on February 29, 1956, in Rochester, Michigan, Wuornos spent her childhood in neighboring Troy, a Detroit suburb. Her mother, Diane Wuornos, was 14 years old when she married Aileen's father, 18-year-old Leo Pittman, on June 3, 1954. On March 14, 1955, Diane gave birth to Aileen's older brother Keith. After less than two years of marriage, and two months before Aileen was born, Diane filed for divorce. She gave birth to Aileen at the age of 16.
One evening in January 1960, when Wuornos was almost four years old, Diane left the children with a babysitter and called to announce that she would not return, leaving them in the care of their maternal grandparents, Lauri and Britta Wuornos, who legally adopted Keith and Aileen on March 18, 1960. Both grandparents had alcoholism. Wuornos never met her father. In 1967, Leo Pittman was sentenced to life imprisonment for kidnapping and raping a seven-year-old girl. Pittman, diagnosed with schizophrenia, died by suicide by hanging in prison on January 30, 1969.

grok_lead: Aileen Carol Wuornos (February 29, 1956 â October 9, 2002) was an American serial killer convicted of murdering seven men in Florida. Between late 1989 and early 1990, Wuornos, who supported herself through prostitution, targeted middle-aged male clients along highways, robbing them after shooting them to death with a.22-caliber pistol and abandoning their vehicles and bodies in wooded areas. She and her companion Tyria Moore pawned items stolen from the victims to sustain themselves. Arrested in January 1991 following a tip, Wuornos initially confessed to the killings but claimed self-defense, alleging the men had attempted to rape her; Moore testified against her in exchange for immunity, corroborating details of the crimes. Convicted in six separate trials, she received death sentences for the murders of Richard Mallory, David Spears, Charles Carskaddon, Troy Burress, Dick Humphreys, and Walter Antonio, pleading no contest to a seventh; appeals citing mental incompetence were rejected by courts, including the Florida Supreme Court and U.S. Supreme Court. Wuornos fired her legal team shortly before her October 2002 execution by lethal injection at Florida State Prison, declaring the men "trying to kill me" and insisting on proceeding without further delays; her case highlighted rare instances of female serial homicide, driven by financial motive and escalating violence rather than sexual predation typical in male counterparts.
